name: Tonkotsu Ramen
description: Thin, springy noodles in a milky-white pork bone broth that is rich, creamy and packed with umami. Topped with melt-in-the-mouth chashu pork, crunchy wood ear mushrooms, nori and plenty of spring onion, this is a bowl that stays with you after the very first taste.
origin: Pork bone ramen was born in the city of Kurume and rose to fame through the ramen shops of Hakata (Fukuoka) on the island of Kyushu around the 1930s–1940s. Today it is one of the most beloved styles of ramen in Japan and around the world.
cooking_style: Hard-boiled bone broth, braised pork, blanched noodles

ingredients.name: Pork leg bones, cut into pieces
Pork belly, in one piece (for chashu)

steps: Blanch the leg bones and trotters in boiling water for 10 minutes, discard the water, then rinse each piece thoroughly under running water to remove clotted blood and scum.

Put the bones and trotters in a large pot with 4 litres of water, the smashed ginger, half the garlic and the green tops of the leek. Keep at a hard, rolling boil for about 8 hours (do not reduce to a simmer), topping up with boiling water from time to time, until the broth turns milky white and slightly thick.

While the bones cook, roll the pork belly tightly, tie it with string and sear until golden on all sides. Braise it with the soy sauce, mirin, 300 ml water and the remaining garlic over low heat for 90 minutes, turning occasionally; let cool, slice thinly and keep the braising liquid as the seasoning base (tare).

Boil the eggs for exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds, plunge straight into iced water, peel and marinate in the braising liquid for at least 2 hours for soft-boiled, well-seasoned eggs. Soak the wood ear mushrooms until softened, boil until cooked and cut into strips.
Strain the broth through a fine sieve. Put 2 tbsp of braising liquid and 1/2 tsp salt in each bowl, ladle in about 350 ml of boiling broth, stir well and taste to adjust.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of boiling water for 1–2 minutes depending on how firm you like them, shake off as much water as possible and add to the bowls. Top with chashu, halved eggs, wood ear mushrooms, finely chopped spring onion and nori, and serve piping hot.

name: Salmon Nigiri Sushi
description: Glossy orange slices of fresh, buttery salmon draped over still-warm vinegared rice. A light dip in soy sauce with a touch of fiery wasabi is all it takes to appreciate the refinement of Japanese cuisine.
origin: Nigiri sushi (hand-pressed sushi) was born in Edo, today's Tokyo, in the early 19th century as a fast food sold at roadside stalls. Raw salmon only became a popular sushi topping in the 1980s, thanks to farmed salmon imported from Norway.
cooking_style: Vinegared rice, sliced raw fish, hand-pressed
steps: Gently rinse the rice several times until the water runs clear, drain, soak for 30 minutes, then cook with 180 ml water. Once cooked, let it steam for another 10 minutes.

Mix the rice vinegar, sugar and salt and warm until fully dissolved. Turn the hot rice out into a wide tray, drizzle the vinegar mixture evenly over it and fold it through with a wooden paddle using cutting strokes so the grains stay intact, fanning as you go until the rice is just slightly warm. Cover with a damp cloth.

Keep the salmon well chilled. Using a long, sharp knife, slice diagonally against the grain into 16 slices about 5 mm thick and 7 cm long, roughly 15 g each, drawing the knife in one smooth stroke for a glossy cut surface.

Dip your hands in a bowl of water with a little vinegar so the rice does not stick, take about 20 g of rice and gently shape it into an oval, without packing it too tightly so it falls apart nicely in the mouth.

Lay a slice of fish in your palm, dab a little wasabi in the centre, place the rice on top and press lightly with two fingers. Turn it over so the fish is on top and press the sides so the fish hugs the rice.
Arrange the sushi on a plate and serve immediately, dipping the fish side into soy sauce and eating pink ginger in between to cleanse the palate.

name: Sashimi
description: Pristine slices of raw fish cut with masterful knife work: deep red tuna, pale pink and richly marbled belly, and translucent white sea bream with its skin still on. A light dip in soy sauce and wasabi is all it takes to taste the pure sweetness of the sea.
origin: Sashimi has been part of Japanese cuisine since the Muromachi period (14th–16th centuries) and became widespread in the Edo period as soy sauce came into common use. The dish embodies the philosophy of respecting the natural flavour of ingredients.
serving_note: 1 serving, about 200 g of fish (15–18 slices)

ingredients.name: Sashimi-grade tuna (lean red meat and belly)
Red sea bream (tai) fillet, skin on
Other white fish fillet or sashimi-grade salmon
Boiling water and iced water (for treating the fish skin)

steps: Use only fish sold specifically for eating raw that has been properly deep-frozen. Thaw slowly in the fridge, pat thoroughly dry with kitchen paper and keep chilled until slicing.
Peel the daikon, shred it into very fine threads and soak in iced water for 10 minutes until crisp and white, then squeeze dry.

Place the sea bream skin side up on a tilted chopping board and cover with a sheet of kitchen paper. Pour boiling water over the skin so it tightens, then plunge immediately into iced water, lift out and pat dry; this softens the skin and brings out its richness.

Use a long, very sharp knife. For the tuna, cut perpendicular to the grain into slices 8–10 mm thick, drawing the knife in one long stroke from heel to tip without sawing. For the sea bream and white fish, angle the knife and cut thin slanted slices 4–5 mm thick.
Pile the daikon into small mounds on a chilled plate or wooden tray, lean the shiso leaves against them and arrange the fish in groups by type, the slices slightly overlapping.
Serve straight away while the fish is still cold. To eat, place a little wasabi on a slice and dip one corner into soy sauce.

name: Tempura
description: Prawns and vegetables in a whisper-thin batter, fried quickly in hot oil for a crisp, airy, lace-light shell while the inside keeps all its fresh sweetness. Dipped in warm tentsuyu with grated daikon, this fried dish is clean-tasting and never greasy.
origin: The technique of batter-frying was brought to Nagasaki in the 16th century by Portuguese missionaries and traders. By the Edo period, tempura had become a famous Tokyo street food, and it was gradually elevated to fine dining.
serving_note: 1 plate of 3 prawns and vegetables, about 200 g

ingredients.name: Tiger prawns or large whiteleg prawns

steps: Make the tentsuyu dipping sauce: boil the dashi, soy sauce and mirin for 1 minute, then keep warm. Grate the daikon finely and squeeze gently to remove some liquid.

Peel the prawns, leaving the tails on, and devein. Make 4–5 shallow cuts across the underside and press gently on the back so the prawns lie straight. Cut the sweet potato and squash into 7 mm slices, halve the aubergine lengthwise and score it into a fan, and cut a cross into the mushroom caps. Pat all the ingredients dry.

Beat the chilled egg with the iced water. Sift in the flour and cornflour and stir roughly with chopsticks 8–10 times, leaving the batter lumpy; overmixing develops gluten and makes the coating chewy. Set the bowl of batter over a bowl of ice to keep it cold.

Heat the oil to 170°C. Dust the vegetables with a very thin layer of dry flour, dip into the batter and lower into the oil, frying for 2–3 minutes until crisp and pale golden. Fry in batches that cover no more than half the oil surface so the temperature does not drop.
Raise the heat to 180°C, hold the prawns by the tail, dip them in the batter and fry for 1.5–2 minutes. Skim stray bits of batter from the oil regularly so it does not burn.
Drain the tempura on a rack and serve immediately while hot and crisp, dipped in the tentsuyu with grated daikon stirred in.

name: Kitsune Udon
description: Thick, round, snow-white udon noodles, soft yet chewy, in a delicately sweet dashi broth, crowned with a juicy piece of sweet simmered fried tofu. A light, warming bowl that suits breakfast as well as chilly days.
origin: A signature noodle dish of Osaka that appeared in the late 19th century. The name kitsune (fox) comes from Japanese folklore, which holds that foxes adore fried tofu.

ingredients.name: Regular Japanese soy sauce (for simmering the tofu)

steps: Make the dashi: soak the kombu in 1 litre of water for 30 minutes, heat over medium heat and remove the kombu just before it boils. Add the bonito flakes, turn off the heat, wait 2 minutes for the flakes to sink, then strain off the clear broth.

Blanch the fried tofu in boiling water for 1 minute to remove excess oil, then press gently to drain. Simmer the tofu with 200 ml dashi, the sugar, regular soy sauce and 1 tbsp mirin over low heat for 10–12 minutes, until the liquid has almost evaporated and the tofu is evenly infused with the sweet-savoury flavour.
Heat the remaining 800 ml dashi with the light soy sauce, 2 tbsp mirin and the salt until gently simmering, and taste to adjust.
Cook the udon in boiling water according to the packet instructions (about 1 minute for frozen, about 3 minutes for fresh), drain and divide between two bowls.
Pour over hot broth to cover the noodles, top with the simmered tofu, sprinkle with finely chopped spring onion and a little shichimi, and enjoy straight away.

name: Tempura Soba
description: Buckwheat noodles with a toasty, nutty aroma in a deep soy-based broth, topped with a golden, crispy fritter of vegetables and shrimp (kakiage). As the batter slowly soaks up the broth, it creates a uniquely rich, savoury flavour.
origin: Soba has been an everyday noodle dish closely tied to Tokyo since the Edo period, when standing noodle stalls sprang up all over the city. The Japanese also eat soba on New Year's Eve (toshikoshi soba) to wish for a long life.
cooking_style: Dashi broth, crispy fried, blanched noodles
steps: Heat the dashi with the soy sauce, mirin and sugar until gently simmering, then keep hot over low heat. Soak the wakame in water for 5 minutes until rehydrated and squeeze dry.
Thinly slice the onion, cut the carrot into matchsticks and pat the shrimp dry. Toss everything with 1 tbsp of dry tempura flour so it is evenly coated.
Mix the remaining tempura flour with the ice-cold water, stirring just a few times (a lumpy batter is fine), then fold gently into the vegetable and shrimp mixture.
Heat the oil to 170°C. Using a ladle, gently slide portions of the mixture into the oil to form flat rounds and fry for about 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp, then drain on a rack.

Cook the soba in a large pot of boiling water for the time on the packet (usually 4–5 minutes), rinse under cold running water, rubbing gently to remove the starch, then dip briefly in boiling water to reheat.
Divide the noodles between bowls, pour over the hot broth and top with the tempura fritter, wakame and thinly sliced onion. Eat immediately while the fritter is still crisp.

name: Tonkatsu (Breaded Pork Cutlet)
description: A thick pork loin cutlet coated in panko and fried to a deep golden brown, shatteringly crisp outside yet tender and juicy within. Served with cool, crunchy shredded cabbage, steamed rice and a rich, tangy-sweet tonkatsu sauce.
origin: Tonkatsu first appeared at a Western-style restaurant in Ginza, Tokyo in 1899, adapted from the European breaded cutlet. Over more than a century it has become fully Japanese and a familiar set meal.
serving_note: 1 set of 150 g fried pork, rice and shredded cabbage
steps: Shred the cabbage very finely, soak in iced water for 10 minutes until crisp, then drain. Stir together the Worcestershire sauce, ketchup, oyster sauce and sugar to make the tonkatsu sauce.

With the tip of a knife, cut through the sinew between the lean meat and fat in a few places so the meat does not curl when fried, pound lightly to an even thickness, then season both sides with salt and pepper.
Dredge the pork in flour and shake off the excess, dip into beaten egg, then coat completely in panko, pressing gently so the crumbs adhere well. Let rest for 5 minutes.

Heat the oil to 170°C and fry the pork for about 3 minutes per side until evenly golden brown. Lift out and stand it on its edge on a rack for 3–4 minutes to drain and let the residual heat finish cooking the centre.
Cut the pork into 2 cm strips and arrange on a plate with the shredded cabbage and lemon wedge. Drizzle the tonkatsu sauce over the pork and serve with hot steamed rice.

name: Japanese Curry Rice
description: A smooth, thick brown curry sauce, fragrant with spice yet mellow, sweet and only mildly hot, simmered with tender beef, potatoes and carrots and served beside sticky white rice. Add a little sweet, crunchy fukujinzuke pickle for the true taste of Japanese home cooking.
origin: Curry arrived in Japan in the late 19th century via the British navy, which had learned the dish in India, and was reworked into a thick sauce eaten with rice. The arrival of boxed curry roux in the 1950s made kare raisu one of Japan's national dishes.
steps: Cook the rice. Cut the beef into 3 cm cubes, the onions into wedges and the carrot into diagonal chunks; peel and quarter the potatoes and keep them in water so they do not discolour. Finely chop the garlic and ginger and finely grate the apple.

Heat the oil in a heavy pot, sear the beef until browned on all sides, then remove. Add the onions, garlic and ginger and saute over medium heat for 8–10 minutes until the onions are soft, golden and sweet.

Return the beef to the pot with the carrot and 800 ml water, bring to the boil and skim off all the foam. Cover and simmer over low heat for 40 minutes. Add the potatoes and grated apple and simmer for another 15 minutes until the beef and potatoes are tender.

Turn off the heat, break the curry roux into pieces, drop it into the pot and stir until completely dissolved. Return to low heat and cook for another 5–10 minutes, stirring along the bottom to prevent scorching, until the sauce is smooth and thick.
Spoon rice onto one side of the plate, ladle curry onto the other and add a little fukujinzuke on the side. Curry left overnight and reheated tastes even richer.

name: Gyudon (Beef Rice Bowl)
description: Thinly sliced beef and onions simmered until tender in a mildly sweet sauce of dashi, soy sauce and mirin, piled generously over a bowl of steaming white rice. Quick, cheap, filling and full of flavour, gyudon is a go-to meal for Japanese office workers at any hour of the day.
origin: Gyudon grew out of the Meiji-era beef hot pot gyunabe ladled over rice. The Yoshinoya chain, which opened at the Nihonbashi fish market in Tokyo in 1899, turned it into an icon of Japanese fast food.
cooking_style: Quick-simmered in sauce, served over rice
steps: Cut the onion into wedges about 1 cm thick. Cut the beef into 5 cm pieces.
Put the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, sake and sugar in a deep frying pan, bring to the boil, then add the onion and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes until soft and translucent.

Scatter the beef into the pan, separating the slices with chopsticks, then add the grated ginger. Simmer gently for 4–5 minutes, skimming off the foam, until the beef is tender and has taken on the colour of the sauce; do not overcook or the beef will turn tough.
Spoon hot rice into bowls, cover the surface with the beef and onion and drizzle over a few extra spoonfuls of sauce.
Top with red pickled ginger and a sprinkle of shichimi. It can be served with a soft poached egg and a bowl of miso soup.

name: Omurice (Omelette Rice)
description: Tangy-sweet ketchup chicken fried rice wrapped in a glossy golden omelette as smooth as silk, finished with a bright red ribbon of ketchup. This Japanese take on a Western dish is easy to love, pretty to look at and adored by children and adults alike.
origin: Omurice is a yoshoku dish (Japanese-style Western food) born in the early 20th century, usually credited to the Rengatei restaurant in Ginza, Tokyo and Hokkyokusei in Osaka. The name combines omelette and rice.
steps: Dice the chicken into 1 cm cubes and finely chop the onion. Melt half the butter in a frying pan, saute the onion until translucent, then add the chicken and cook through, seasoning with a little salt and pepper.

Push the chicken to one side, add 4 tbsp ketchup to the empty part of the pan and stir for about 1 minute to mellow its acidity and bring out its aroma. Add the cold rice and soy sauce and toss briskly until the grains are separate and coloured orange-red. Divide the rice into two portions.

Beat 2 eggs with 1 tbsp milk and a pinch of salt. Heat a 20–22 cm non-stick pan with a little oil and butter, pour in the eggs and stir quickly with chopsticks for about 10 seconds until about 70% set, with the top still slightly runny.

Turn off the heat, place one portion of rice lengthwise down the centre of the omelette and fold the two edges over to wrap the rice. Slide it to the edge of the pan, flip it upside down onto a plate and use kitchen paper to shape it into a neat oval.
Repeat with the remaining portion. Pipe the rest of the ketchup over the omelettes and serve hot.

name: California Roll
description: An inside-out sushi roll with the rice on the outside, coated in fish roe or toasted sesame, wrapped around crab sticks, creamy ripe avocado and crisp, cool cucumber. Its mild, approachable flavour makes it perfect for sushi newcomers.
origin: The California roll was created by Japanese chefs in North America around the 1960s–1970s, who hid the seaweed inside and swapped raw fish for avocado and crab to suit Western diners. It paved the way for the global wave of fusion sushi.
cooking_style: Vinegared rice, rolled with a bamboo mat
serving_note: 1 roll cut into 8 pieces, about 260 g

ingredients.name: Flying fish roe (tobiko) or toasted sesame seeds
Japanese soy sauce, wasabi, pickled pink ginger

steps: Rinse the rice well and cook with 360 ml water. Dissolve the vinegar, sugar and salt, then fold into the hot rice with cutting strokes, fanning as you mix until the rice is just slightly warm.

Peel and stone the avocado and cut it lengthwise into 1 cm slices. Deseed the cucumber and cut into long batons. Split the crab sticks in half lengthwise. Cut each nori sheet in half to get 4 half sheets.

Wrap a bamboo mat in cling film. Lay a half sheet of nori on the mat and, with wet hands, spread about 150 g of rice over it to cover completely, sprinkle evenly with roe or sesame, then flip it over so the rice side faces down.

Lay the crab sticks, avocado and cucumber along the edge of the nori nearest you and pipe on a line of mayonnaise. Lift the mat and roll firmly away from you, squeezing gently to form an even cylinder.
With a sharp knife dipped in water, cut each roll into 8 pieces, wiping the blade after each cut for clean slices. Arrange on a plate and serve with soy sauce, wasabi and pink ginger.

name: Sukiyaki Hot Pot
description: Melt-in-the-mouth slices of marbled beef simmered in a shallow cast-iron pot in a rich, sweet soy sauce broth, alongside grilled tofu, napa cabbage, mushrooms and shirataki noodles that soak up all the flavour. Dipping the piping-hot beef into a bowl of beaten raw egg is the classic way to enjoy it.
origin: Sukiyaki became popular in the Meiji period (late 19th century), when the Japanese began eating beef again after centuries of abstention. The Kanto style simmers the ingredients in a premixed sauce, while the Kansai style sears the beef with sugar first and then adds soy sauce.

ingredients.name: Thinly sliced marbled beef (sirloin or short plate)
Fresh eggs, safe to eat raw

steps: Make the warishita sauce: boil the sake and mirin for 1 minute to cook off some of the alcohol, add the soy sauce and sugar, stir until dissolved, then turn off the heat.

Cut the napa cabbage into 5 cm pieces, slice the leeks diagonally 1.5 cm thick, score a decorative pattern into the shiitake caps, trim the enoki roots, cut the tofu into 3 cm pieces and halve the chrysanthemum greens. Blanch the shirataki in boiling water for 2 minutes to remove its odour, then cut into shorter lengths.

Set the shallow cast-iron pot on a burner in the middle of the table, heat it and rub the beef suet all over the bottom. Sear the first few slices of beef with some leek until fragrant, pour over a ladle of sauce and enjoy these slices straight away.

Arrange the cabbage, leeks, mushrooms, tofu and shirataki in separate clusters in the pot and pour in enough sauce to come about a third of the way up the ingredients. Keep the shirataki away from the beef, as it tends to toughen the meat. Simmer gently for 5–7 minutes so the vegetables absorb the flavour.
Add the beef and chrysanthemum greens last, cooking for just 30–60 seconds until the beef just changes colour so it stays tender.

Each diner cracks a raw egg into their own bowl, beats it and dips the hot beef and vegetables into the egg before eating. Keep adding ingredients and sauce throughout the meal; if the sauce becomes too strong, dilute it with a little water or dashi.

name: Okonomiyaki (Japanese Savoury Pancake)
description: A thick griddled pancake made from batter, egg and plenty of finely chopped cabbage, topped with crisply seared pork belly. It is brushed with a sweet-savoury brown sauce, striped with mayonnaise and sprinkled with green seaweed and fragrant bonito flakes.
origin: Okonomiyaki means grill what you like, and it became popular in Osaka and Hiroshima after World War II, when wheat flour replaced rice as a staple. The Osaka style mixes all the ingredients into the batter, while the Hiroshima style stacks them in layers with fried noodles.
cooking_style: Mixed batter, griddled on a flat-top
steps: Whisk the flour with the dashi and grated yam until smooth, then let the batter rest in the fridge for 15 minutes. Cut the cabbage into short shreds about 3 cm long and finely chop the spring onions.

Divide the batter between two bowls. Add half the cabbage, 1 egg, spring onion, tenkasu and red ginger to each bowl. Mix by gently lifting from the bottom with a spoon, without overmixing, so the pancake stays light and fluffy.

Heat a heavy-based frying pan or flat griddle over medium heat (about 200°C) and brush with a thin layer of oil. Pour in the mixture to form a round 2 cm thick, lay 3 slices of pork belly on top and cook for 4–5 minutes until the base is golden.

Flip the pancake decisively with two spatulas, cover and cook for another 5 minutes over medium-low heat until the pork is crisp and the inside is cooked through. Never press the pancake flat. Flip once more and cook for 2 more minutes.
Brush okonomiyaki sauce over the top, pipe on thin lines of mayonnaise, then sprinkle with aonori and bonito flakes. Cut into squares with the spatula and eat hot, straight from the pan.

name: Takoyaki (Octopus Balls)
description: Perfectly round, piping-hot balls with a fragrant golden shell, a soft, molten centre and a chewy piece of octopus inside. Topped with sweet-savoury takoyaki sauce, mayonnaise, green seaweed and bonito flakes dancing in the heat, they are Japanese street snacking at its best.
origin: Takoyaki was created in 1935 by Endo Tomekichi, who ran a street stall in Osaka. Since then it has become an icon of Kansai street food and appears at every festival in Japan.
steps: Beat the eggs with the dashi, soy sauce and salt, then sift in the flour and whisk into a thin, smooth batter. Cut the octopus into 1.5 cm pieces and finely chop the spring onions and red ginger.
Heat the takoyaki pan over medium heat and brush oil generously into every hole and over the surface of the pan. The pan is hot enough when a drop of batter sizzles.
Pour in the batter until it floods the whole surface of the pan, drop a piece of octopus into each hole, then sprinkle the tenkasu, spring onion and red ginger evenly over the top.

After about 2–3 minutes, once the bottoms have set, use a skewer to cut through the batter overflowing between the holes, turn each ball 90 degrees and tuck the excess batter inside so the raw batter runs down to form a sphere.
Keep turning the balls continuously for another 5–6 minutes until they are evenly round with a golden-brown, slightly crisp shell.
Arrange on a plate, brush with takoyaki sauce, squeeze over mayonnaise and sprinkle with aonori and bonito flakes. Eat hot, but carefully, as the filling is very hot.

name: Chicken Karaage
description: Chicken thigh marinated in soy sauce, ginger and garlic, given a thin potato starch coating and fried twice for a shatteringly crisp crust and a juicy interior. Add a squeeze of lemon and a dip of mayonnaise for an irresistible drinking snack or quick bite.
origin: Karaage frying was influenced by Chinese cuisine and spread widely in Japan after World War II; Oita Prefecture on the island of Kyushu is considered the capital of this fried chicken. Today karaage is everywhere, from izakaya pubs to convenience stores and bento boxes.
steps: Cut the chicken into pieces about 4 cm square, keeping the skin on. Mix the chicken with the soy sauce, sake, ginger, garlic and sesame oil, massage well and marinate in the fridge for 30 minutes.
Combine the potato starch and flour. Lift the chicken out of the marinade to drain, roll each piece in the flour mixture and squeeze lightly so the skin wraps the meat and the coating sticks evenly.
Heat the oil to 160°C and fry the chicken in small batches for 3–4 minutes until pale golden, then transfer to a rack and rest for 4 minutes so the residual heat keeps cooking the inside.
Raise the oil temperature to 190°C and fry the chicken a second time for 45–60 seconds until golden brown and very crisp. Drain well.
Arrange the chicken on a bed of shredded cabbage with a lemon wedge and mayonnaise; squeeze the lemon over the chicken just before eating.

name: Onigiri (Rice Balls)
description: Triangles of fragrant, sticky white rice hiding a filling of savoury grilled salmon or tangy pickled plum, wrapped in a strip of crisp nori. Compact, filling and easy to take anywhere, this is Japan's favourite grab-and-go food.
origin: Rice balls appeared in Japan more than a thousand years ago and once served as provisions for samurai and long-distance travellers. Today onigiri are sold in every convenience store with dozens of different fillings.
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, soak for 30 minutes, then cook with 360 ml water. Once cooked, let it steam for another 10 minutes and fluff it up.

Rub 1/2 tsp salt over the salmon, leave for 10 minutes, then pat dry. Pan-fry or grill the salmon for 3–4 minutes per side until cooked, remove the skin and bones and flake it. Remove the stones from the pickled plums.
Cut each nori sheet lengthwise into 3 strips to get 6 strips.

Wet both hands and rub a pinch of salt into your palms. Take about 110 g of warm rice, make a hollow in the centre, add a spoonful of salmon or half a pickled plum and mound the rice over to enclose the filling.

Cup your top hand into a V shape and press gently while turning the rice ball 3–4 times to form a triangle. Press just enough for the rice to hold together, not too tightly, so the grains stay loose when you bite into it.
Wrap a strip of nori around the base of each rice ball just before eating so the nori stays crisp, and sprinkle with a few toasted sesame seeds if you like.

name: Miso Soup
description: A hot bowl of soup with the gently salty, deeply aromatic flavour of fermented soybean paste dissolved in delicately sweet dashi, finished with silky soft tofu and wakame seaweed. Light, comforting and an almost indispensable part of any Japanese meal.
origin: Miso soup has been part of Japanese meals since the Kamakura period (12th–14th centuries) and is part of the traditional ichiju-sansai meal (one soup, three dishes). Each region uses its own miso, from the sweet white miso of Kyoto to the deep red miso of Nagoya.
steps: Soak the kombu in 800 ml water for about 20 minutes, then heat over medium heat and remove the kombu just before the water boils. Add the bonito flakes, turn off the heat, wait 2 minutes, then strain off the clear dashi.
Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes until rehydrated, then squeeze dry. Cut the tofu into 1 cm cubes and finely chop the spring onions.
Reheat the dashi, add the tofu and wakame and cook for 1–2 minutes over low heat.

Turn the heat down to the lowest setting. Put the miso in a ladle or small sieve, lower it into the pot and stir with chopsticks so it gradually dissolves into the broth. Do not let the soup boil again once the miso is in, to preserve its full aroma.
Ladle the soup into bowls, sprinkle with spring onion and serve hot with rice.

name: Mochi Daifuku
description: A pure white round cake with a fine dusting of starch, its soft, stretchy glutinous rice skin wrapped around a smooth, delicately sweet red bean filling. Savour it with a cup of hot green tea for the full Japanese tea-time experience.
origin: Daifuku appeared in Edo (Tokyo) in the late 18th century; its name means great fortune, so it is often given as a gift for good luck. This original sweet has inspired many variations, such as strawberry daifuku and mochi ice cream.
cooking_style: Cooked bean paste, steamed rice dough, hand-shaped
steps: Soak the red beans for at least 4 hours or overnight. Boil the beans for 5 minutes, then discard the first water to reduce bitterness, add fresh water to cover by 3 cm and simmer over low heat for 50–60 minutes until the beans are very soft and crush easily when pressed.

Blend the beans with a little of the cooking liquid, then press through a fine sieve to remove the skins. Put the smooth bean puree in a pan with 100 g sugar and the salt and cook over medium-low heat for 10–15 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste is thick and pulls together into a mass. Let cool, divide into 8 balls of about 30 g and keep in the fridge.

Mix the glutinous rice flour with 30 g sugar and 150 ml water until smooth. Cover loosely with cling film and microwave at 600W for 1 minute, take out and stir with a wet spatula, microwave for another 1 minute, stir again, then microwave for 30 more seconds until the dough is translucent, sticky and stretchy. Without a microwave, steam the dough for 15 minutes, stirring once halfway.
Dust a tray with a thick layer of cornflour, turn the hot mochi dough out onto it, dust the top with more starch and use a dough scraper to divide it into 8 portions while still warm.

Flatten each portion into a round 7–8 cm across, thicker in the centre than at the edges. Place a ball of filling in the middle, pull the edges up and pinch to seal, roll into a ball and place seam side down. Brush off the excess starch.
Eat the same day while the skin is still soft and stretchy; do not refrigerate, as the rice skin will harden.

name: Dorayaki (Red Bean Pancakes)
description: Two fluffy, honey-scented pancakes with evenly glossy brown tops, sandwiching a sweet, nutty red bean filling. This is the very pancake Doraemon the robot cat adores, a treat tied to the childhood of generations.
origin: Dorayaki in today's two-layer form was introduced by the Usagiya confectionery in Ueno, Tokyo in 1914. The name comes from the word dora, meaning gong, after the cake's flat, round shape.
cooking_style: Whisked egg batter, cooked in a dry pan
steps: Whisk the eggs with the sugar and honey for 3–4 minutes until light, fluffy and pale. Sift in the flour and baking powder, mix until just combined, then cover tightly and rest the batter in the fridge for 15 minutes.
Add the water a spoonful at a time, stirring gently, until the batter falls from the lifted whisk in a continuous ribbon.
Heat a non-stick pan over low heat. Soak a piece of kitchen paper in oil and wipe it over the pan, removing almost all the oil so the pancakes brown evenly and smoothly.

Scoop about 2 tbsp of batter and pour it from a height onto one spot so it spreads into a round 8 cm across. Cook for about 2 minutes until tiny bubbles appear on the surface, then flip and cook for another 30–40 seconds, remove and cover with a damp cloth so the pancakes do not dry out. Repeat with the remaining batter to make 16 pancakes.
Spread about 40 g of red bean paste on the inner side of one pancake, piling it thicker in the centre, then top with a second pancake and press gently around the edges to seal.
Wrap each one in cling film and leave for about 30 minutes so the pancakes become moist and soft and absorb the flavour before serving.

name: Matcha Latte
description: Jade-green matcha powder whisked with warm water, then combined with silky hot milk for a gently astringent, lightly creamy drink with a clean, sweet finish. Both energising and calming, it looks beautiful with latte art in the milk foam on top.
origin: Matcha has been closely tied to the Japanese tea ceremony since the 12th century, with tea from Uji in Kyoto the most famous. The matcha latte is a modern twist that combines traditional tea with Western milky coffee culture, spreading worldwide from the early 2000s.
cooking_style: Whisked tea, mixed with hot milk
steps: Sift the matcha powder through a fine sieve into a bowl or wide-mouthed glass so it does not clump.

Pour in water at about 80°C (boiling water will make the tea bitter) and whisk quickly in an M-shaped motion with a bamboo chasen or handheld milk frother for 20–30 seconds, until the tea is fully dissolved and topped with a fine foam.
Add the sugar or honey to the tea and stir until dissolved.
Heat the milk to about 65°C without letting it boil, then froth with a milk frother until smooth and increased by half in volume.

Pour the tea into a glass, tilt it and slowly pour in the hot milk, finally lowering the jug to create a design in the foam. For an iced version, fill the glass with ice, pour in cold milk, then pour the matcha on top for two layers of colour.
